subject: 🔎 Dem's SpaceX probe
body_html:
Plus: York Space Systems' robot bet | Thursday, November 12, 2026

Axios Future of Defense
By Thomas Novelly · Nov 12, 2026

Good morning, y'all! It's Thursday and we've got a ton of news to unpack.

🎤 But, first: We're one week out from the Axios Future of Defense Summit! I'm excited to dive into the latest defense and space trends with some big names.

🌎 Watch this space: Let's see what's at stake in a congressional Elon Musk probe, reveal some exclusive space industry news and glance at Anduril's satellite tech.
 
 
1 big thing: SpaceX scrutiny
 

Photo illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Photos: Getty Images
 

The new Democratic congressional majority is vowing a slew of investigations into Elon Musk's business empire — potentially putting the military's vast portfolio of contracts with SpaceX under the microscope.

Why it matters: Attempts to hold Musk accountable will run up against a basic reality that for critical military and space missions, the government has no replacement for SpaceX — and likely won't for years.

The big picture: How the military became so reliant on a single company may itself be an area of inquiry, congressional aides and former U.S. officials told me.

  • "There's enough questionable appearances here that I think it's in everybody's interest to go find out what really happened," a former Pentagon official told me, referring to Musk's political influence and the federal contracts SpaceX has accrued.
  • Practically, it will be years before SpaceX competitors offer technology that allows the Defense Department to diversify to non-Musk companies.
  • Musk this week almost dared the government to try, writing on X that he was "happy to cancel any that the government doesn't want. Just say the word!"

By the numbers: Since Musk left the U.S. government as an adviser in May 2025, SpaceX has netted at least $10 billion in new contracts, according to a new report from the left-leaning nonprofit Democracy Defenders Fund.

  • That includes two major Space Force contracts: One for nearly $2.3 billion to build a sprawling network of communication satellites and another nearly $4.2 billion award to develop a space-based missile tracking radar.
  • In September, NASA awarded $946 million to SpaceX for three missions to transport astronauts to the International Space Station.
  • Nearly 94% of all orbital U.S. launches were from SpaceX last year, per the American Enterprise Institute's data. So far, in 2026, Musk's rockets have accounted for roughly 90% of those missions.

Zoom in: The new Congress is likely to investigate Musk's role in throttling Starlink over Ukraine and the circumstances surrounding SpaceX contracts.

  • "How many hearings have the Republicans held focusing on SpaceX and its abuses of its contracts or its actions in Ukraine? Zero," one Democratic Senate aide said.
  • The Senate Armed Services Committee, which helps craft defense spending policy, is also likely "to have a different posture towards how [the Defense Department] handles its SpaceX contracts" starting in January, the aide said.

What they're saying: Clayton Swope, a senior space fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said there's been a long-standing fear in the defense community that the military has put "all eggs in the SpaceX basket."

  • "That's always been kind of an underlying current, even within the Pentagon, that we're very uncomfortable with reliance on one vendor," Swope said. "But, then, here we are."

State of play: Despite those concerns, SpaceX's satellite and rocket technology has allowed the U.S. to maintain its superiority in space.

  • But competitors that lag behind now see an opening for the Pentagon to adopt alternatives.
  • SpaceX's looming retirement of the Falcon 9 rocket, for example, has reportedly left the Space Force in a bind for future launches.
  • This week, the Defense Department's Office of Strategic Capital signed a $150 million conditional loan commitment with SpaceX competitor Rocket Lab "to meet growing commercial and national security demand for access to space."

Yes, but: Dave Cavossa, the Commercial Space Federation's president, told me "Starlink and Starshield are one-of-a-kind capabilities" and said that competitors, like Amazon Leo, are a year or two away from becoming operational.

  • "SpaceX has built a massive lead today ... The new entrants have to run really hard to catch up," Cavossa said.

Reality check: Musk still has the firm backing of Trump and his allies.

  • Shortly before the election, the president vowed to "protect" him amid Democratic scrutiny.
  • New White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller can now weigh in on Musk's government dealings after his wife left her role with SpaceX, The Atlantic reported.
  • "He's untouchable," Fox News host Jesse Watters said of Musk this week. "He's reached a level in this country that, a subpoena? A hearing? It's nothing."

The White House and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment.

The bottom line: Another former Pentagon official argued that the military's heavy reliance on Musk is precisely why he deserves to be investigated.

  • "Strong national security requires actual competition to both keep costs competitive and to prevent amassing of power in any one individual or company," the person said.
 
 
2. Exclusive: York Space robots
 

York Space Systems plans to acquire an Australian robot maker. Photo: Courtesy/York Space Systems
 

York Space Systems is planning to buy an Australia-based robot maker, marking the publicly-traded U.S. company's expansion into unmanned technology.

Why it matters: Space and autonomous systems are the future of modern warfare. York wants to weave the two together.

Driving the news: The Colorado-based space company plans to acquire Outlook Industries, a private firm, which will be the base for York Terrestrial Systems.

  • The company's first robot offering will be Shadow: a four-wheeled ground rover built in the U.S. that will be connected to the firm's space-based network.

What he's saying: York Space Systems CEO Dirk Wallinger told me in future wars, especially against an adversary like China, space-based connectivity for unmanned platforms will be the difference between having superiority and being left behind.

  • "There's also the recognition that the space layer is what it takes to fight these global battles," Wallinger said. "This is a different battle, and you absolutely need space to do it."

The big picture: York wants autonomy to play a major role in its existing constellation of satellites and in its emerging robot fleet.

  • York's planned purchase of Outlook follows the company's acquisitions of ALL.SPACE mobile satellite technology and ATLAS Space Operations' ground station software.
  • The company is now also offering a software suite that automates satellite mission planning and day-to-day constellation operations, among other tasks.
  • During a Dec. 15 demo, York plans to show the Shadow robot driving itself and deploying a drone, Wallinger said.

What's next: York is also interested in expanding its robot fleet offerings to unmanned boats and even underwater vessels.

  • "We're starting with Outlook Shadow there and the unmanned system, but it doesn't need to stop there," Wallinger said. "It's more about leveraging our space ecosystem so that we can have the architecture that the U.S. needs going forward in the future."
 
 
3. Exclusive: Trusted Space expansion
 

Illustration: Natalie Peeples/Axios
 

Trusted Space, a space software company, has purchased Falcon ExoDynamics, a firm that builds technology for maneuverable satellites.

Why it matters: As the number of satellites surges, there likely won't be enough Space Force Guardians to monitor and operate them all.

  • Investors see autonomous software and dynamic satellites as key developments in orbital warfare.

Between the lines: The purchase, guided by Washington Harbour Partners, puts autonomy-focused hardware and software together.

What he's saying: Trusted Space CEO Robert MacMillan told me "there are a small number of Guardians that are flying an ever-increasing number of satellites." The cognitive load will eventually become a burden, he said.

  • "Have we reached that tipping point yet? I don't think so," MacMillan said. "Is it coming, as we go to more and more proliferated constellations? Certainly."

Follow the money: Trusted Space and Falcon ExoDynamics have both netted space contracts recently.

  • In August, the Air Force Research Laboratory awarded an almost $15 million contract to Virginia-based Trusted Space for autonomous satellite experiments.
  • That same month, California's Falcon ExoDynamics was part of a team that secured a $24 million joint Defense Innovation Unit and Space Development Agency award to pull dead satellites out of orbit.

What's next: MacMillan said Trusted Space is focused on building out a new satellite prototype and is working towards orbital experiments.

  • "We've got to move quickly, demonstrate our capability, establish that trust and autonomy with our operators, so that we can meet the national security needs for the United States," he said.

4. Quick hits
 

Hegseth (center left) tours AFRICOM with Gen. Michael Langley (center right) and his leadership team. Photo: Courtesy of the Office of the Secretary of Defense
 

⬟ ICYMI: House Republicans blocked an impeachment effort on Tuesday evening against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

What they're saying: Hegseth and Pentagon officials were touting the win on Tuesday evening. Vice President JD Vance said on X "impeachment has become a ridiculous show."

💭 My thought bubble: We can't forget what my Axios colleague Kate Santaliz pointed out "the reprieve is probably short-lived: Democrats are all but guaranteed to force the issue again" next year.

🚀 Planet Labs will hitch rides for its imaging satellites aboard Stoke Space's yet-to-be-launched reusable Nova Pathfinder rocket, the companies announced on Monday.

Why it matters: Planet has around 200 of its satellites on orbit, but that constellation won't grow if they can't reliably get them into space.

💭 My thought bubble: The looming retirement of SpaceX's stalwart Falcon 9 rocket is clearly pushing satellite providers to place bets.

🇬🇧 A new British-built military satellite, the Titania, is now on orbit, the U.K. confirmed in a Saturday announcement.

What he's saying: "The new space age is here ... and it is critical for our national security and military operations," U.K. Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting said in a statement.

💭 My thought bubble: Compared to the U.S., there's a surprising amount of detail and transparency in the U.K.'s news release. I'll be keeping an eye on the nation's orbital buildup.
 
 
5. Check this out
 

An image of the moon taken from the Long Wave Infrared Space Sensor on Anduril's satellite. Photo: Courtesy/Anduril
 

Anduril Industries used a new sensor aboard its independently-funded satellite to snap a picture of the moon.

Why it matters: The defense firm is finally revealing details about its emerging space technology.

Between the lines: The above image was taken with the satellite's Long-Wave Infrared Space Sensor, which uses heat signatures to capture pictures.

  • The sensor was aboard the Anduril-216 satellite that was launched in July.
  • Other Anduril payloads aboard the satellite included an edge computing processor for orbital missions and a power management system.
